## Introduction

Welcome to ***Welcomed by the New Colossus: An Atlas of American Communities***.  This is Isabela Carvajal Rios, and I will be showing you a few curious facts about the American Communities that live in the USA, and especially Colombian-Americans. 

Everybody knows United States of America is known as the land of dreams and opportunities, and as a Colombian myself, I will explain more in detail about my people in this country and where they reside. This edition will also cover NYC buildings, the density of the population here, the American community diversity in the country, and a bit of history. 

To make this possible, the data used was sourced from the Census (ACS), NYC neighborhood maps, and PLUTO (Primary Land Use Tax Lot Output). 

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)
library(httr2)
library(gt)
library(ggiraph)
library(patchwork)

if (!dir.exists(file.path("data", "mp03"))) {
  dir.create(file.path("data", "mp03"), recursive = TRUE)
}
  col_yellow <- "#FCD116"
col_blue   <- "#003893"
col_red    <- "#CE1126"
```
## Data Acquisition

### Metro Areas (CBSA)

CBSA stands for Core Based Statistical Area, and it is the census name for an area and the surroundings where people live and commute from every day. In this case we will be using New York area and the surroundings where people live.

```{r}
cbsa_file <- file.path("data", "mp03", "cbsa_colombian.shp")

if (!file.exists(cbsa_file)) {
  cbsa_raw <- get_acs(
    geography = "cbsa",
    variables = c(total = "B01003_001", colombian = "B03001_020"),
    year = 2024,
    survey = "acs5",
    output = "wide",
    geometry = TRUE
  )
  write_sf(cbsa_raw, cbsa_file)
}

cbsa <- read_sf(cbsa_file)
```

### NYC Census Tracts

A tract is a small area that the Census uses to collect data, and each tract is between 1,200 to 8,000 people. So when tracts are mentioned, they refer to small areas of a city. 
I downloaded the total population and the Colombian-American population for every tract in the 5 boroughs (including the map shapes).

```{r}
tract_file <- file.path("data", "mp03", "nyc_tracts_colombian.shp")

if (!file.exists(tract_file)) {
  tracts_raw <- get_acs(
    geography = "tract",
    variables = c(total = "B01003_001", colombian = "B03001_020"),
    state = "NY",
    county = c("New York", "Kings", "Queens", "Bronx", "Richmond"),
    year = 2024,
    survey = "acs5",
    output = "wide",
    geometry = TRUE
  )
  write_sf(tracts_raw, tract_file)
}

nyc_tracts <- read_sf(tract_file)
```

### NYC Neighborhoods (NTAs)

NTA's are the New York City's official neighborhoods, this data is collected by the Department of City Planning and it includes all the names. I downloaded the zip file from NYC Planning.

```{r}
load_nyc_nta <- function() {
  data_dir <- file.path("data", "mp03")
  if (!dir.exists(data_dir)) dir.create(data_dir, recursive = TRUE)

  nta_url <- "https://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/dcp/assets/files/zip/data-tools/bytes/neighborhood-tabulation-areas/nynta2020_26d.zip"
  zip_file <- file.path(data_dir, "nyc_nta.zip")
  if (!file.exists(zip_file)) {
    download.file(nta_url, destfile = zip_file, mode = "wb")
  }

  unzip_dir <- file.path(data_dir, "nyc_nta")
  if (!dir.exists(unzip_dir)) unzip(zip_file, exdir = unzip_dir)

  shp_path <- list.files(unzip_dir, pattern = "\\.shp$",
                         recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)

  read_sf(shp_path[1]) |>
    select(BoroName, NTA2020, NTAName, NTAType)
}

nyc_nta <- load_nyc_nta()
```

### Aggregating Tracts to Neighborhoods
Census tracts and NTAs are drawn by different agencies, so because some tracts may fall in two neighborhoods we assigned each tract to the neighborhood it overlaps the most instead of splitting them, and then added up the population count for each neighborhood. This makes it easier to have the actual neighborhood name instead of an ID tract and give us a better sense of the data. 

```{r}
# 1. Put tracts in the same CRS as the NTA map, drop empty (water) tracts
nyc_tracts <- nyc_tracts |>
  filter(!st_is_empty(geometry)) |>
  st_transform(st_crs(nyc_nta))

# 2. Spatial join: each tract gets the NTA it overlaps most
tract_nta <- st_join(nyc_tracts, nyc_nta,
                     join = st_intersects, largest = TRUE)

# 3. Drop geometry and add up tracts within each NTA
nta_pop <- tract_nta |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(NTA2020) |>
  summarize(total = sum(totalE, na.rm = TRUE),
            colombian = sum(colombianE, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(pct_colombian = colombian / total)

# 4. Reconnect to the NTA shapes
nyc_nta_pop <- nyc_nta |>
  left_join(nta_pop, by = "NTA2020")
```

### NYC Buildings (PLUTO)

```{r}
pluto_file <- file.path("data", "mp03", "pluto.csv")

if (!file.exists(pluto_file)) {
  base_url <- "https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/64uk-42ks.csv"
  page_size <- 50000
  offset <- 0
  pages <- list()

  repeat {
    resp <- request(base_url) |>
      req_url_query(
        `$select` = "bbl,borough,bct2020,landuse,unitsres,unitstotal,resarea,officearea,comarea,bldgarea,numfloors",
        `$order`  = "bbl",
        `$limit`  = page_size,
        `$offset` = offset
      ) |>
      req_perform()

    page <- read_csv(I(resp_body_string(resp)),
                     col_types = cols(.default = "c"))
    pages[[length(pages) + 1]] <- page
    message("Downloaded rows ", offset + 1, " to ", offset + nrow(page))

    if (nrow(page) < page_size) break
    offset <- offset + page_size
  }

  bind_rows(pages) |> write_csv(pluto_file)
}

pluto <- read_csv(pluto_file, col_types = cols(bct2020 = "c", bbl = "c"))
```

## Data Integration
Now we have to join the buildings to population by census tract. As of right now PLUTO's ID is the borough digit + the tract, and the Census ID is NY + County+ the tract. The purpose of this join is so PLUTO is added by tract and match the ID's we will be using later. 

```{r}
# Borough digit -> county FIPS
boro_fips <- c("1" = "061", "2" = "005", "3" = "047",
               "4" = "081", "5" = "085")

pluto_tract <- pluto |>
  filter(!is.na(bct2020)) |>
  mutate(
    GEOID = paste0("36", unname(boro_fips[str_sub(bct2020, 1, 1)]),
                   str_sub(bct2020, 2, 7)),
    across(c(officearea, unitsres, resarea, comarea, bldgarea),
           ~ replace_na(.x, 0))
  ) |>
  group_by(GEOID) |>
  summarize(
    office_area = sum(officearea),
    res_units   = sum(unitsres),
    res_area    = sum(resarea),
    com_area    = sum(comarea),
    bldg_area   = sum(bldgarea),
        max_floors  = if (all(is.na(numfloors))) NA_real_ else max(numfloors, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_floors  = mean(numfloors, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Join to census tracts (keeps NTA info from Step 5)
tracts_full <- tract_nta |>
  left_join(pluto_tract, by = "GEOID")
```

## Exploratory Data Analysis

### NYC's Built Environment

#### Where is NYC's office space?
(Which NYC census tract has the most office floor area in NYC?)

Office space matters for understanding where people live, because office areas have less population density, they have a lot of office buildings and commercial areas, but not as many resident buildings. People have to commute to go to work when they don't live in the area. 

(A census tract is a small area the Census Bureau uses to collect data, and each tract has an ID.)

```{r}
top_office <- tracts_full |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  slice_max(office_area, n = 5) |>
  select(GEOID, NTAName, BoroName, office_area)

top_office |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "NYC Census Tracts with the Most Office Space",
    subtitle = "Total office floor area, square feet"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    GEOID = "Tract ID",
    NTAName = "Neighborhood",
    BoroName = "Borough",
    office_area = "Office Area (sq ft)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(office_area, decimals = 0) |>
    data_color(columns = office_area, palette = "Blues") |>
  tab_source_note("Source: NYC PLUTO")
```

In the table above we can see the top 5 NYC Census Tracts with the most office space. The top tract, in `r top_office$NTAName[1]`, has
`r scales::comma(top_office$office_area[1])` square feet of office space. In this top 5 we can see `r knitr::combine_words(unique(top_office$BoroName))` is the borough for all the top tracts. We can also see these 2 areas `r knitr::combine_words(unique(top_office$NTAName))` have the most concentration of office space.

#### Where are NYC's homes?
(Which NTA has the most residential units?)

```{r}
nta_units <- tracts_full |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(NTA2020, NTAName, BoroName) |>
  summarize(res_units = sum(res_units, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(res_units, n = 10)

p_units <- ggplot(nta_units,
       aes(x = res_units,
           y = fct_reorder(NTAName, res_units),
           fill = BoroName,
           tooltip = paste0(NTAName, " (", BoroName, ")\n",
                            scales::comma(res_units), " units"),
           data_id = NTA2020)) +
  geom_col_interactive() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "NYC Neighborhoods with the Most Residential Units",
    subtitle = "Top 10 Neighborhood Tabulation Areas · hover for details",
    x = "Residential units", y = NULL, fill = "Borough",
    caption = "Source: NYC PLUTO; NYC Dept. of City Planning NTAs"
  ) +
    theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")

girafe(ggobj = p_units, width_svg = 9, height_svg = 5,
       options = list(opts_sizing(rescale = TRUE)))
```
The chart above gives us a visual on the top 10 neighborhoods in NYC with the most residential units. We can see `r sum(nta_units$BoroName == "Manhattan")` out of 10 neighborhoods are located in the `r knitr::combine_words(unique(nta_units$BoroName))` borough.  

`r nta_units$NTAName[1]` is the neighborhood with the most residential units totaling: `r scales::comma(nta_units$res_units[1])`. This neighborhood has tall buildings so there are many units on the same piece of land one on top of each other, using less territory.

#### Where is NYC most crowded?
(Which NYC census tract has the highest population density, measured as population per square foot of residential space? Do your answers change if you measure by population per residential unit?)

```{r}
density <- tracts_full |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(res_units >= 50, res_area > 0, totalE > 0) |>
  mutate(
    pop_per_1k_sqft = totalE / res_area * 1000,
    pop_per_unit    = totalE / res_units
  )

top_sqft <- density |> slice_max(pop_per_1k_sqft, n = 5) |>
  mutate(measure = "Ranked by people per 1,000 sq ft")
top_unit <- density |> slice_max(pop_per_unit, n = 5) |>
  mutate(measure = "Ranked by people per unit")

bind_rows(top_sqft, top_unit) |>
  select(measure, GEOID, NTAName, BoroName, totalE,
         pop_per_1k_sqft, pop_per_unit) |>
  gt(groupname_col = "measure") |>
  tab_header(
    title = "NYC's Most Densely Populated Census Tracts",
    subtitle = "Two ways of measuring residential crowding"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    GEOID = "Tract ID", NTAName = "Neighborhood", BoroName = "Borough",
    totalE = "Population",
    pop_per_1k_sqft = "People per 1,000 sq ft",
    pop_per_unit = "People per unit"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(totalE, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(c(pop_per_1k_sqft, pop_per_unit), decimals = 2) |>
  data_color(columns = c(pop_per_1k_sqft, pop_per_unit), palette = "Oranges") |>
  tab_source_note("Source: ACS 2020–2024 5-year; NYC PLUTO. Tracts with fewer than 50 residential units excluded.")
```
Above you can see the most densely populated census tract table is divided in two, the top is calculating the tracts ranked by people per 1,000 sq ft, and the bottom part is ranked by people per unit. 

The neighborhood `r top_sqft$NTAName[1]` in the borough `r top_sqft$BoroName[1]` is the most dense tract with `r round(top_sqft$pop_per_1k_sqft[1], 2)` people per 1,000 sq ft, it is also the most dense in the bottom table with `r round(top_unit$pop_per_unit[1], 2)` people per unit.  

The neighborhoods and boroughs may vary between both tables because the top one is measuring population density per 1,000 sq ft: very small units that can hold more people in the same area. And the bottom table is measuring people by units, since there may be large families in apartments, both contributing to population density. Keeping both tables gives a better insight of the type of buildings in the area and how many people live there. (For this analysis any tracts with under 50 units were excluded.)


### Colombian-Americans Across the US

#### Where else do Colombians concentrate?
(What 5 metro areas, other than NYC, have the largest share of population that identify with your ancestry of interest?)

```{r}
cbsa_share <- cbsa |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(str_detect(NAME, "Metro Area"),   # metro areas only, no micro areas
         GEOID != "35620") |>              # 35620 = New York metro
  mutate(pct_colombian = colombianE / totalE) |>
  slice_max(pct_colombian, n = 5)

cbsa_share |>
  select(NAME, totalE, colombianE, pct_colombian) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Metro Areas with the Highest Share of Colombian-Americans",
    subtitle = "Excluding the New York metro area"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    NAME = "Metro Area", totalE = "Total Population",
    colombianE = "Colombian-Americans", pct_colombian = "Share Colombian"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(c(totalE, colombianE), decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_percent(pct_colombian, decimals = 1) |>
  data_color(columns = pct_colombian, palette = "YlOrRd") |>
  tab_source_note("Source: ACS 2020–2024 5-year, table B03001")
```

In the table above we can see the metro areas in the USA with the highest share of Colombian Americans (Colombian immigrants, US- born children and grand children that identify as Colombian, since the census is self reported). This table excludes the New York metro area.

The metro area that have the highest share of Colombian- Americans is `r cbsa_share$NAME[1]`, it holds  `r scales::comma(cbsa_share$colombianE[1])` Colmbian-American people, and a share of `r scales::percent(cbsa_share$pct_colombian[1], accuracy = 0.1)`. In the state of Florida only there are `r sum(str_detect(cbsa_share$NAME, ", FL"))` of the top 5 metros.


#### A closer look at one city
(The distribution of ancestries in a large non-NYC city of Miami-Fort Lauderdale- West Palm Beach area.)

```{r}
# Pick the most populous metro from the Q4 top 5
focus <- cbsa_share |> slice_max(totalE, n = 1)

origin_file <- file.path("data", "mp03", "cbsa_hispanic_origin.csv")

if (!file.exists(origin_file)) {
  origin_raw <- get_acs(
    geography = "cbsa",
    variables = c(
      total = "B03001_001", not_hispanic = "B03001_002",
      mexican = "B03001_004", puerto_rican = "B03001_005",
      cuban = "B03001_006", dominican = "B03001_007",
      central_american = "B03001_008", south_american = "B03001_016",
      colombian = "B03001_020", other_hispanic = "B03001_027"
    ),
    year = 2024,
    survey = "acs5"
  )
  write_csv(origin_raw, origin_file)
}

origin <- read_csv(origin_file, col_types = cols(GEOID = "c"))

city_mix <- origin |>
  filter(GEOID == focus$GEOID) |>
  select(variable, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = estimate) |>
  mutate(other_south_american = south_american - colombian) |>
  select(-south_american) |>
  pivot_longer(-total, names_to = "group", values_to = "pop") |>
  mutate(
    share = pop / total,
    group = str_to_title(str_replace_all(group, "_", " "))
  )

ggplot(city_mix, aes(x = share, y = fct_reorder(group, share),
                     fill = group == "Colombian")) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent,
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey70", col_blue)) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Who lives in the", str_remove(focus$NAME, " Metro Area"), "area?"),
    subtitle = "Share of residents by Hispanic origin · Colombian highlighted",
    x = "Share of metro population", y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: ACS 2020–2024 5-year, table B03001"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")
```

In the chart above we can see the breakdown of who lives in the Miami-Fort Lauderdale- West Palm Beach area. When added up, `r scales::percent(1 - city_mix$share[city_mix$group == "Not Hispanic"], accuracy = 0.1)` of the population is Hispanic. 

The largest Hispanic group is the Cuban with `r scales::percent(city_mix$share[city_mix$group == "Cuban"], accuracy = 0.1)` of the population. Colombian is the second largest single country group with a share of `r scales::percent(city_mix$share[city_mix$group == "Colombian"], accuracy = 0.1)` of the population. The reason Cuban population is the highest group is due to the Cuban migration that took place after the 1959 Cuban Revolution  ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_migration_to_Miami)).

#### How concentrated are Colombian-Americans?
(As a percentage of all US residents who identify as Colombian- American, how many live in NY and how many live in other major metro areas)

```{r}
us_file <- file.path("data", "mp03", "us_colombian.csv")

if (!file.exists(us_file)) {
  us_raw <- get_acs(
    geography = "us",
    variables = c(colombian = "B03001_020"),
    year = 2024,
    survey = "acs5",
    output = "wide"
  )
  write_csv(us_raw, us_file)
}

us_colombian <- read_csv(us_file, show_col_types = FALSE)$colombianE

metro_share <- cbsa |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(share_of_us = colombianE / us_colombian) |>
  slice_max(colombianE, n = 10) |>
  mutate(cum_share = cumsum(share_of_us))

nyc_share <- metro_share$share_of_us[metro_share$GEOID == "35620"]

metro_share |>
  select(NAME, colombianE, share_of_us, cum_share) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Where Do Colombian-Americans Live?",
    subtitle = "Top 10 metro areas by Colombian-American population"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    NAME = "Metro Area", colombianE = "Colombian-Americans",
    share_of_us = "Share of US Total", cum_share = "Cumulative Share"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(colombianE, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_percent(c(share_of_us, cum_share), decimals = 1) |>
  data_color(columns = share_of_us, palette = "Greens") |>
  tab_source_note("Source: ACS 2020–2024 5-year, table B03001")
```

In the table above we can see both New York-Newark-Jersey City, NY-NJ Metro Area and Miami-Fort Lauderdale-West Palm Beach, FL Metro Area are almost tied, and together they hold `r scales::percent(metro_share$cum_share[2], accuracy = 0.1)` of the share of Colombian-Americans in the US. So we can conclude that over a third of the people who consider themselves as Colombian-Americans are more concentrated in NJ/NY and Miami. And almost half is concentrated in NJ/Ny and Florida's three metros with `r scales::percent(nyc_share + sum(metro_share$share_of_us[str_detect(metro_share$NAME, ", FL")]), accuracy = 0.1)`. 

The top 10 metros in the table hold about `r scales::percent(max(metro_share$cum_share), accuracy = 0.1)` of the Colombian-Americans. And if we compare Florida to New York we can see Florida's three largest metros are the home to more Colombian-Americans with `r scales::comma(sum(metro_share$colombianE[str_detect(metro_share$NAME, ", FL")]))` Colombians, vs New York with `r scales::comma(metro_share$colombianE[metro_share$GEOID == "35620"])` Colombians.


### Population and Housing

#### Do more homes mean more people?
(Do we observe a roughly linear relationship between population and housing (units or area) across NYC tracts or is the relationship more complex?)

```{r}
cor_units <- cor(density$res_units, density$totalE)
cor_area  <- cor(density$res_area, density$totalE)

ggplot(density, aes(x = res_units, y = totalE)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = BoroName), alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "black") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Population vs. Housing Units Across NYC Census Tracts",
    subtitle = "Black = straight-line fit · Red dashed = flexible (loess) fit",
    x = "Residential units", y = "Population", color = "Borough",
    caption = "Source: ACS 2020–2024 5-year; NYC PLUTO"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")
```


In the scatter plot above we can visualize the amount of residential units and the population. The black line shows the straight line fit and the red line bends to follow the data we have. 

We can see that up to the 4000 residential units the relationship is fairly linear, and after the 5000 units the red line starts to bend down.This tells us that up to the 4000 units more homes are equivalent to more people, and after the 5000 units, more units have less people than the black line had anticipated (even though after 6000 units the red curve is relying on few points only). The correlation between units and population is `r round(cor_units, 2)`, and this number shows us the data correlation is strong. When comparing population with residential are we get `r round(cor_area, 2)`, which is almost the same as the correlation between units and population, both telling us that if there are more homes there are more people. 


#### Where are the tallest buildings?
(The NTA's with highest buildings) 

```{r}
# Give each PLUTO lot its tract GEOID and neighborhood
pluto_nta <- pluto |>
  filter(!is.na(bct2020), numfloors > 0) |>
  mutate(GEOID = paste0("36", unname(boro_fips[str_sub(bct2020, 1, 1)]),
                        str_sub(bct2020, 2, 7))) |>
  inner_join(tract_nta |> st_drop_geometry() |>
               select(GEOID, NTA2020, NTAName, BoroName),
             by = "GEOID")

tallest <- pluto_nta |>
  group_by(NTAName, BoroName) |>
  summarize(
    avg_floors  = mean(numfloors),
    max_floors  = max(numfloors),
    pct_20plus  = mean(numfloors >= 20),
    n_buildings = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(n_buildings >= 50) |>
  slice_max(avg_floors, n = 10)

tallest |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "NYC's Tallest Neighborhoods",
    subtitle = "Ranked by average number of floors per building"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    NTAName = "Neighborhood", BoroName = "Borough",
    avg_floors = "Avg. Floors", max_floors = "Tallest (floors)",
    pct_20plus = "Share 20+ Floors", n_buildings = "Buildings"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(avg_floors, decimals = 1) |>
  fmt_number(c(max_floors, n_buildings), decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_percent(pct_20plus, decimals = 0) |>
  data_color(columns = avg_floors, palette = "Purples") |>
  tab_source_note("Source: NYC PLUTO. Lots with no recorded floors excluded.")
```

In the table above we can see that New York City's top 10 tallest neighborhoods `r sum(tallest$BoroName == "Manhattan")` of 10 are in `r knitr::combine_words(unique(tallest$BoroName))` The tallest neighborhood is `r tallest$NTAName[1]` with an average of `r round(tallest$avg_floors[1], 1)` floors, and the tenth tallest neighborhood is a lot shorter with an average of `r round(tallest$avg_floors[10], 1)` floors, less than half (`r scales::percent(tallest$avg_floors[10] / tallest$avg_floors[1], accuracy = 1)`). 

Fidi and Midtown have the tallest buildings with `r tallest$max_floors[1]` floors on the tallest in Fidi and `r tallest$max_floors[tallest$NTAName == "Midtown South-Flatiron-Union Square"]` floors in Midtown South-Flatiron-Union Square, but they have an average of `r round(tallest$avg_floors[1], 1)` and `r round(tallest$avg_floors[tallest$NTAName == "Midtown South-Flatiron-Union Square"], 1)` floors because the rest of the buildings in the area are not so tall. Both of this areas are office districts. In this table I excluded neighborhoods with less than 50 buildings so that the data was showing the reality of an area and not only a tall building in an area with few buildings where the averages could appear inflated.

#### Mapping density across the city
(How population density varies across NYC)

```{r}
nta_density <- tracts_full |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(NTA2020) |>
  summarize(pop = sum(totalE, na.rm = TRUE),
            res_area = sum(res_area, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(pop_per_1k_sqft = if_else(res_area > 0, pop / res_area * 1000, NA_real_))

density_map <- nyc_nta |>
  left_join(nta_density, by = "NTA2020") |>
  mutate(pop_per_1k_sqft = if_else(NTAType == "0", pop_per_1k_sqft, NA_real_))  # parks, airports etc. → grey

p_density <- ggplot(density_map) +
  geom_sf_interactive(
    aes(fill = pop_per_1k_sqft,
        tooltip = paste0(NTAName, " (", BoroName, ")\n",
                         round(pop_per_1k_sqft, 2), " people per 1,000 sq ft"),
        data_id = NTA2020),
    color = "white", linewidth = 0.1
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, na.value = "grey85",
                       name = "People per\n1,000 sq ft") +
  labs(
    title = "Residential Population Density Across NYC Neighborhoods",
    subtitle = "Residents per 1,000 sq ft of residential floor area · grey = parks, airports, cemeteries",
    caption = "Source: ACS 2020–2024 5-year; NYC PLUTO; NYC DCP NTAs"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")

girafe(ggobj = p_density, width_svg = 8, height_svg = 8,
       options = list(opts_sizing(rescale = TRUE)))
```

In the map above we can see the neighborhoods with more residents per 1000 sq ft are a darker color than the areas with less residents density. Surprisingly Manhattan is light colors which reflect there is low density there (even if it has the highest buildings), compared to `r density_map$BoroName[which.max(density_map$pop_per_1k_sqft)]` where there central part of the map is highlighted in darker tones. Brooklyn is also highlighted in darker colors as well. 

After hovering over the map we can see the location with the most resident density is `r density_map$NTAName[which.max(density_map$pop_per_1k_sqft)]` in `r density_map$BoroName[which.max(density_map$pop_per_1k_sqft)]` with `r round(max(density_map$pop_per_1k_sqft, na.rm = TRUE), 2)` people per 1000 square feet. 

Circling back to the data analyzed in previous sections, the densest neighborhood is also in the middle of where the highest concentration of Colombian-Americans are in Queens. 

#### Who lives in commercial areas?
(How many New Yorkers live in areas that could be described as 'primarily commercial')

```{r}
# Definition: a tract is "primarily commercial" when commercial floor area
# is more than a given share of all building floor area
commercial <- tracts_full |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(bldg_area > 0) |>
  mutate(com_share = com_area / bldg_area)

nyc_pop <- sum(tracts_full$totalE, na.rm = TRUE)

threshold_tbl <- tibble(threshold = c(0.5, 0.6, 0.75)) |>
  mutate(
    tracts    = map_int(threshold, ~ sum(commercial$com_share > .x)),
    residents = map_dbl(threshold, ~ sum(commercial$totalE[commercial$com_share > .x])),
    pct_nyc   = residents / nyc_pop
  )

pop_commercial <- threshold_tbl$residents[threshold_tbl$threshold == 0.5]

threshold_tbl |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "New Yorkers Living in Primarily Commercial Tracts",
    subtitle = "How the answer changes with the definition of 'primarily commercial'"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    threshold = "Commercial share of floor area above",
    tracts = "Tracts", residents = "Residents", pct_nyc = "Share of NYC"
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(threshold, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(c(tracts, residents), decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_percent(pct_nyc, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_source_note("Source: ACS 2020–2024 5-year; NYC PLUTO (comarea / bldgarea)")
```

In the table above we can see the amount of New Yorker's living in primary commercial tracts. The table also shows data for 3 different angles, depending on what the reader considers as 'primarily commercial'.

For the first example I am considering 'primarily commercial' if more than `r scales::percent(threshold_tbl$threshold[1])` of the floor area is commercial. The data shows that around `r scales::percent(threshold_tbl$pct_nyc[1], accuracy = 0.1)` of New Yorker's live in primarily commercial tracts, with a total of about `r scales::comma(pop_commercial)` people and `r threshold_tbl$tracts[1]` tracts. 

If we consider 'primarily commercial' when more than `r scales::percent(threshold_tbl$threshold[3])` of the share is commercial, then there would be `r scales::percent(threshold_tbl$pct_nyc[3], accuracy = 0.1)` of New Yorker's living in these areas, with `r scales::comma(threshold_tbl$residents[3])` residents and `r threshold_tbl$tracts[3]` tracts.


## Atlas of Communities Entry: Colombian-Americans 🇨🇴

Colombians started migrating to the United States of America in the 1950's, after the civil war in Colombia. Many people left the country because the quality of life was not the best, there was a lot of poverty, and there was an Act passed in 1965 that made it easier for Colombians to move here and start again. Then between the 1980's and 1990's many more Colombians left Colombia to escape from the violence and drug dealing era.

During the 1970's many Colombians that moved to the USA decided to settle in Jackson Heights in Queens and during the 1980's many Colombians settled in Miami. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombian_Americans))

Colombian-Americans are all the people that consider themselves or identify as Colombian immigrants, US- born children and grand children, since the census is self reported.
But where do Colombian- Americans live now? Please take a look at the following map:

### Colombian America
```{r}
us_metros <- cbsa |>
  filter(str_detect(NAME, "Metro Area")) |>
  mutate(pct_colombian = colombianE / totalE) |>
  tigris::shift_geometry()   # moves Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico under the mainland

p_us <- ggplot(us_metros) +
  geom_sf_interactive(
    aes(fill = pct_colombian,
        tooltip = paste0(str_remove(NAME, " Metro Area"), "\n",
                         scales::comma(colombianE), " Colombian-Americans (",
                         scales::percent(pct_colombian, accuracy = 0.1), ")"),
        data_id = GEOID),
    color = "white", linewidth = 0.05
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = col_yellow, high = col_red, transform = "sqrt",
                      labels = scales::percent, name = "Share\nColombian") +
  labs(
    title = "Colombian-Americans Across US Metro Areas",
    subtitle = "Share of metro population identifying as Colombian · hover for details",
    caption = "Source: ACS 2020–2024 5-year, table B03001"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")

girafe(ggobj = p_us, width_svg = 10, height_svg = 6,
       options = list(opts_sizing(rescale = TRUE)))
```

The USA has a total of `r scales::comma(us_colombian)` Colombians. We can see that there are two main areas in the map with high shares of Colombians, they are noticeably darker shades of orange and almost red located in the Miami area with a share of `r scales::percent(cbsa_share$pct_colombian[1], accuracy = 0.1)` of it's population, and new york area is home to `r scales::percent(nyc_share, accuracy = 0.1)` of all the Colombian-Americans in the USA. Most Colombians are located in the East coast, and the rest of the country has very few Colombian-Americans in relation with the two areas mentioned.

### Colombian New York

Now let's take a look at the Colombians in New York in the map below:

```{r}
col_nta <- nyc_nta_pop |>
  mutate(pct_colombian = if_else(NTAType == "0", pct_colombian, NA_real_))

top_col_nta <- col_nta |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  slice_max(colombian, n = 10)

p_col_map <- ggplot(col_nta) +
  geom_sf_interactive(
    aes(fill = pct_colombian,
        tooltip = paste0(NTAName, "\n", scales::comma(colombian),
                         " Colombian-Americans (",
                         scales::percent(pct_colombian, accuracy = 0.1), ")"),
        data_id = NTA2020),
    color = "white", linewidth = 0.1
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = col_yellow, high = col_red, na.value = "grey90",
                      labels = scales::percent, name = "Share\nColombian") +
  theme_void()

p_col_bar <- ggplot(top_col_nta,
                    aes(x = colombian, y = fct_reorder(NTAName, colombian),
                        tooltip = paste0(NTAName, ": ", scales::comma(colombian)),
                        data_id = NTA2020)) +
  geom_col_interactive(fill = col_blue) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "Colombian-Americans", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

girafe(
  ggobj = (p_col_map + p_col_bar + plot_layout(widths = c(1.4, 1))) +
    plot_annotation(
      title = "Where Colombian New Yorkers Live",
      subtitle = "Share of residents by neighborhood · top 10 neighborhoods by count · hover to link panels",
      caption = "Source: ACS 2020–2024 5-year, table B03001; NYC DCP NTAs"
    ),
  width_svg = 11, height_svg = 6,
  options = list(opts_hover(css = "stroke:black;stroke-width:2px;"),
                 opts_sizing(rescale = TRUE))
)
```
In this map we can  visualize the map of NYC and also a bar chart of the top 10 neighborhoods with the most Colombian-Americans, and `r sum(top_col_nta$BoroName == "Queens")` of the top 10 are in Queens.

We can see that the top New York neighborhood with the highest amount of Colombian-Americans is `r top_col_nta$NTAName[1]` with `r scales::comma(top_col_nta$colombian[1])` Colombians, equivalent to a share of `r scales::percent(top_col_nta$pct_colombian[1], accuracy = 0.1)` of the total Jackson Height's population. 
 
To conclude, the New York Metro Area has the most amount of Colombian-Americans, but Miami has the highest concentration of them. Looking back on history, the main migration waves from the 1970's to NY, and in 1980's to Miami defined where Colombian-American people would live in the future, and we can see this clearly in the data analyzed here, because to this day over a third of them are still located in those two places. About `r scales::percent(max(metro_share$cum_share) - metro_share$cum_share[2], accuracy = 0.1)` are located in the top eight metros (after Miami and NY area): Orlando, Houston, Atlanta, Los Angeles, Washington DC, Tampa, Boston, and Chicago, and the rest of them (`r scales::percent(1 - max(metro_share$cum_share), accuracy = 0.1)`) are spread across the United states in smaller metropolitan areas.
